---
title: "Figure 9.2: Total Factor Productivity Relative to the US"
---

![Python: `python/fig-9-2.py`](../images/python/fig-9-2.png)

Annual total factor productivity (TFP) relative to the United States for
four economies, 2000 to 2031. A value of 100 would mean the same TFP as the
United States. The years after the latest data are projections; the chart
draws them in the same way as the history.

**New in this chart:** a legend in one row across the top.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 32 rows (2000 to 2031):

| category | LA7 | EM Asia | EM Europe | Canada |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 | 69.3 | 36.3 | 70.0 | 95.4 |

One column per line, and the years as numbers in `category`. The column
names are exactly the legend labels, so the script can use them for both.

## The script

This is one of the shortest scripts. It is worth reading in full as an
example of the basic pattern that most line charts in the book follow.

### Colours and frame

```python
series_colours = {
    "LA7": "#7030A0",
    "EM Asia": "#00A6AD",
    "EM Europe": "#C65911",
    "Canada": "#404040",
}
```

The order of the dictionary is the order in which the lines are drawn and
the order of the legend entries. A later line is drawn on top of an earlier
one, so Canada, last, lies on top where lines cross.

The call to `new_chart()` sets the title, subtitle and a six-line caption.
`bottom_gap=0.45` is a little larger than usual, because the year labels
below the x-axis are written vertically.

### The drawing

```python
for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xlim(2000, 2031)
ax.set_xticks(range(2000, 2031, 5))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, length=2.8)

set_y_scale(ax, 30, 110, 20)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02), ncol=4,
          handlelength=2.6, handletextpad=0.4, columnspacing=1.0)
```

- **The lines.** One `ax.plot()` per series, with the years on the x-axis.
  `label=series` stores the name for the legend.
- **The x-axis.** The limits are exactly the first and last years, so the
  lines start at the left edge and end at the right edge, with no margin.
  `range(2000, 2031, 5)` gives 2000, 2005, ..., 2030, the years that get a
  label. The range stops before 2031, but the axis runs on to 2031, the last
  data year. `labelrotation=90` writes the labels vertically.
- **The y-axis** runs from 30 to 110 with a tick every 20: 30, 50, 70, 90,
  110. It starts at 30, not zero. In matplotlib, as in Excel, the limits are
  what you set; there is no rule that an axis must include zero. Starting at
  30 gives the lines more height, which is fine for a chart of levels like
  this one. See [The y-scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-y-scale).
- **The legend.** It is centred across the top: `loc="upper center"` means
  the top-centre point of the legend is placed at the anchor, and
  `bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02)` puts the anchor halfway across the plot,
  slightly above its top edge. `ncol=4` puts the four entries in one row.

### Fitting the legend in one row

Four entries side by side are wider than the default spacing allows, so
three arguments are tightened:

| Argument | Meaning | Value here | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `handlelength` | length of the line sample | 2.6 | 2.0 |
| `handletextpad` | gap between sample and text | 0.4 | 0.8 |
| `columnspacing` | gap between columns | 1.0 | 2.0 |

All three are in units of the font size, so they scale if you change the
legend's font size. The line samples are a little longer than the default,
and the gaps much shorter, which lets the row fit within the plot width.
See [Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

## Changing the chart

- **Mark the projections.** To show which years are projections, shade them
  with `ax.axvspan(2026, 2031, color="#EEEEEE", zorder=0)`, or draw the
  projection years as dashed lines with a second `ax.plot()` call per series
  and `linestyle="--"`.
- **Legend in two rows.** Use `ncol=2` and move the anchor down a little, or
  put the legend below the chart with `loc="upper center"` and
  `bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.2)` plus more `bottom_gap`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-9-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-9-2.py"}
"""Figure 9.2: Total Factor Productivity Relative to the US."""
from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-9-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {
    "LA7": "#7030A0",
    "EM Asia": "#00A6AD",
    "EM Europe": "#C65911",
    "Canada": "#404040",
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Total Factor Productivity Relative to the US",
    subtitle="(Percent)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: IMF, World Economic Outlook database; Penn World Table 11.0\n"
        "database; and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Aggregates are purchasing-power-parity GDP- weighted averages.\n"
        "EM = emerging; EM Asia = India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines,\n"
        "Thailand; EM Europe = Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia; LA7 = Latin\n"
        "America 7 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay)."
    ),
    left=0.35,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.45,
)

for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xlim(2000, 2031)
ax.set_xticks(range(2000, 2031, 5))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, length=2.8)

set_y_scale(ax, 30, 110, 20)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02), ncol=4,
          handlelength=2.6, handletextpad=0.4, columnspacing=1.0)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
